title: "Starting Up Front Doesn't Guarentee Strong Finish in NASCAR"

A strong qualifying performance can put a NASCAR driver near the front of the field, but where a driver starts is only part of the story. Once the green flag drops, positions can change dramatically before the checkered flag waves.

An analysis of the 2025 NASCAR Cup Series season found that drivers who started closer to the front generally finished better. However, the relationship between starting and finishing positions was far from perfect, showing that a favorable starting spot doesn't necessarily translate into a strong finish.

While drivers starting in the top five held a noticeable advantage over those starting farther back, several drivers consistently gained positions during races, demonstrating how much the running order can change.


![NASCAR Cup Series racing action](images.jpeg)




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Load NASCAR Cup Series results
cup_results <- load_series("cup")

# Select the 2025 season
nascar_2025 <- cup_results %>%
  filter(
    Season == 2025,
    !is.na(Start),
    !is.na(Finish),
    Start > 0,
    Finish > 0
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    positions_gained = Start - Finish
  )

# Check the dataset
nrow(nascar_2025)
```

## How much does starting position matter?

The relationship between starting position and finishing position was positive but not especially strong during the 2025 NASCAR Cup Series season.

An analysis of Cup Series results found a correlation of .33 between starting and finishing positions. Because lower position numbers represent better results, the positive relationship indicates that drivers starting closer to the front tended to finish closer to the front.

However, the correlation also suggests that starting position alone is not a particularly strong predictor of the final result.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#| label: fig-start-finish
#| fig-cap: "Starting and finishing positions in the 2025 NASCAR Cup Series."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

# Categorize position changes
nascar_2025 <- nascar_2025 %>%
  mutate(
    movement = case_when(
      positions_gained >= 10 ~ "Gained 10+ positions",
      positions_gained <= -10 ~ "Lost 10+ positions",
      TRUE ~ "Within 9 positions"
    )
  )

# Scatterplot
ggplot(nascar_2025,
       aes(x = Start, y = Finish)) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    color = "gray50",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = movement),
    alpha = 0.45,
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Gained 10+ positions" = "#16826D",
      "Lost 10+ positions" = "#D55E42",
      "Within 9 positions" = "#9CA3AF"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_reverse(
    breaks = seq(5, 40, by = 5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Does Starting Position Predict the Finish?",
    subtitle = "2025 NASCAR Cup Series | First place is best",
    x = "Starting position",
    y = "Finishing position",
    color = "Position change",
    caption = "Source: nascaR.data / DriverAverages.com"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The scatterplot illustrates how drivers’ positions changed throughout races. Some drivers starting near the front dropped 10 or more positions by the finish, while others farther back improved by at least 10 spots. 
These differences demonstrate that starting near the front offers an advantage, but it doesn’t eliminate the possibility of losing ground during a race. 
Starting near the front provides an advantage 
(Average finishing position by starting group)
Drivers who started in the top five recorded the best average finishing position among the four starting groups examined. 
During the 2025 season, drivers starting first through fifth finished an average of 14.3. Those starting sixth through 10th averaged 16.5, while drivers starting 11th through 20th averaged 17.9.
Drivers starting 21st or farther back had the worst average finishing position at 22.7
That represents an 8.4-position difference between the top-five starting group and drivers who began 21st or worse. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#| label: fig-starting-groups
#| fig-cap: "Average finishing position by starting group in the 2025 NASCAR Cup Series."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

# Group drivers by their starting positions
starting_groups <- nascar_2025 %>%
  mutate(
    starting_group = cut(
      Start,
      breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 20, Inf),
      labels = c("1-5", "6-10", "11-20", "21+")
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(starting_group) %>%
  summarise(
    average_finish = mean(Finish, na.rm = TRUE),
    driver_race_entries = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# View the group averages
print(starting_groups)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  starting_group average_finish driver_race_entries
  <fct>                   <dbl>               <int>
1 1-5                      14.3                 180
2 6-10                     16.5                 180
3 11-20                    17.9                 360
4 21+                      22.7                 649
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Calculate the difference between top-five
# starters and drivers starting 21st or worse
position_difference <-
  starting_groups$average_finish[
    starting_groups$starting_group == "21+"
  ] -
  starting_groups$average_finish[
    starting_groups$starting_group == "1-5"
  ]

# Create the bar chart
ggplot(
  starting_groups,
  aes(
    x = starting_group,
    y = average_finish,
    fill = starting_group
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.65,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(average_finish, 1)),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "1-5" = "#16826D",
      "6-10" = "#70B4A2",
      "11-20" = "#9CA3AF",
      "21+" = "#D55E42"
    )
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 2.5,
    y = 27,
    label = paste0(
      round(position_difference, 1),
      "-position difference\n",
      "between top-five and 21+ starters"
    ),
    color = "#18453B",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 32),
    breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Starting Up Front Is Linked to Better Finishes",
    subtitle = "Average finishing position by starting group, 2025 NASCAR Cup Series",
    x = "Starting position",
    y = "Average finishing position (lower is better)",
    caption = "Source: nascaR.data / DriverAverages.com"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

The result suggests that starting near the front is associated with a better finish. However, even drivers who begin in the first five positions finished outside of the top 10 on average. 
Although a good starting position can put a driver in a favorable position early, maintaining that advantage through the finish is another challenge. 
Which drivers gained the most ground?
(NASCAR’s biggest position gainers)
Not every driver needs to start near the front to make significant progress during a race.
Among drivers with at least 25 race entries in 2025, Ricky Stenhouse Jr. and John Hunter Nemecheck recorded the largest average position gains, each improving by approximately five positions per race.
Todd Gilliand followed with an average gain of 4.7 positions, while Cody Ware gained 4.5. Ryan Preece rounded out the top five with an average improvement of 3.7 positions



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#| label: fig-driver-gains
#| fig-cap: "Drivers with the largest average position gains per race in 2025."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

# Calculate position gains by driver
driver_gains <- nascar_2025 %>%
  group_by(Driver) %>%
  summarise(
    races = n(),
    average_gain = mean(
      positions_gained,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(races >= 25) %>%
  arrange(desc(average_gain)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

# View the results
print(driver_gains)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Chase Elliot, Ross Chastain, Daniel Suárez, Brad Keselowski and Erik Jones also ranked among the top 10 drivers with the largest average gains. 
These results highlight the ability of drivers to improve their positions after the race begins, even when they don’t start near the front. 
However, average position gains don’t necessarily identify the strongest overall drivers. Competitors starting farther back have more positions available to gain, while those starting near the front have fewer opportunities to move forward. 
The starting grid doesn’t tell the whole story. 
The 2025 NASCAR Cup Series results reveal two important findings: starting closer to the front is associated with better finishes, but the starting grid is far from a guarantee of where drivers will finish. 
The 8.4-position difference between the best and worst starting groups demonstrates the advantage associated with starting near the front. At the same time, the .33 correlation and the position gains recorded by individual drivers highlight how much change between the start and finish of a race. 
Starting position provides an early advantage, but the final running order tells a much more complicated story. 
For NASCAR drivers, qualifying well may be an important first step. The challenge is turning that starting position into a strong result when the checkered flag falls.
